messages.subject: Multiple output formats & caching
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

for my dissertation I need to run models that take a couple of weeks on my computer (stochastic actor oriented models of network change, using rsiena). Hence, I need to use caching.
I typically write in markdown/rmarkdown and need to knit these documents into multiple output formats, e.g. a html website, a LaTeX document for an article I want to publish and a html presentation. Thus, I have at least three different markdown documents.
Is it possible to write an analysis-rmarkdown file with some results chunks, knit this and then access the different, already evaluated, chunks as child documents in the three different markdown documents without having them being evaluated again? As the computations take weeks, I cannot let them be evaluated once per output format.

Or is it possible to tell knitr that it knits the results into markdown/png files that I could then manualy refer to in the three markdown documents and update it by creating a waf/makefile that checks for changes?

You see, I'm a bit confused, but I hope you can help me.

Best and many thanks,
Robert

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Multiple output formats & caching
messages.body_plain:
I recommend setting up one or more R files that do the computations and leave the results in memory. This helps in debugging. Then use another R file that sets up simulation control parameters,  sources the computation files and then explicitly saves the results. "save.image" works for me, but with calculations that take weeks I might consider exchangeable formats for future-proofing (what if you want to share the results later with someone who doesn't use R?). Finally, use knitr to assemble those results into reports as desired.

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Multiple output formats & caching
messages.body_plain:
If it takes a couple of weeks to run your models, you probably don't
want to use knitr's built-in caching feature, because it may be too
sensitive to changes, e.g. you certainly don't want to re-run the code
just because you added a white space in it. Instead, you can run the
code separately, save the results (e.g. save(), saveRDS(), ...), and
load them manually (e.g. load(), readRDS(), ...) into your code
chunks. IMO, knitr's caching is handy for computation that takes a few
minutes to hours, but may not be a good choice for computation that
takes weeks.

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>
Web: http://yihui.name

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Multiple output formats & caching
messages.body_plain:
Thanks all for this thread, I think this highlights some tricky issues that could benefit from larger discussion.  I agree with Jeff and Yihui's comments that direct knitr caching doesn't work well in this circumstance.  As both of their suggestions highlight, this really is a good example of where the research has "outgrown" what can be encapsulated in knitr alone, and a good solution that still preserves the advantages of the dynamic document approach needs to be something + knitr.  I don't think we've had enough discussion or consensus as to what that something should be (not that we need consensus -- but just as knitr has helped make a widely recognized and powerful 'standard' for dynamic documents so far, we could benefit by some similar focus here, as well as perhaps the tacit acknowledgement that research can outgrow stand-alone knitr).

Jeff and Yihui's solutions both involve external R scripts; and many of us use `make` as an one obvious way to stitch together these scripts with the knitr document.  However, make has many drawbacks (e.g. relies on timestamps rather than hashes to identify if files have changed, which is defeated by things like switching branches in git).

Robert, I highly suggest you take a look at Rich FitzJohn's remake package if you are interested in automating this: https://github.com/richfitz/remake .  It's not perfect, but I think it does offer one view of a more scalable approach to tackling this very issue.  I'm still trying to settle on a solution for this problem myself -- so far `remake` is the closest/best thing I've found, but I'd love to hear others thoughts on this.  I found both Jeff and Yihui's comments on how they handle this to be very insightful (e.g. saving images, saving exchangeable formats -- the latter has become much easier for me now that dplyr has me keeping everything in data.frames instead of lists).

Cheers,
Carl

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Multiple output formats & caching
messages.body_plain:
Thank you all for your suggestions! I will have a look at remake. I never heard of it before.

I recently started playing around with Hans Martin von Gaudeckers template for reproducible research, which can be found here: https://github.com/hmgaudecker/econ-project-templates . While I don't understand a lot of the (waf) code, I think it might be helpful in this setting. There are a couple of nice features in this template, such as that it generates a documentation for the project, resolves dependencies as a DAG/ uses clever caching and if possible runs stuff in parallel, e.g. multiple models with different parameters that only depend on the same data but not on each other. Within the template, one just has to call an R-script that knits the rmd/rnw files.

Best,
Robert

messages.body_plain:
I just took a look at your example, and your main issue was that you
have to separate the HTML <body> with the <head>. Here is a hackish
way to achieve that (using regular expressions, which is not
reliable):

ehtml = function(content) {
  content = htmltools::HTML(gsub('^.*?<body\\s*>|</body>.*$', '', content))
  d = htmltools::htmlDependency(
    'TeX4ht', '1.0.0', src = getwd(), stylesheet = 'summarym-enclosed.css')
  htmltools::attachDependencies(content, d)
}

Note summarym-enclosed.css was hard-coded in the function, and you'd
better replace it with a filename automatically elicited from the
HTML. I'm not sure if there is a way for htlatex to produce the body
and css separately, so you don't have to hack at the generated HTML.

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>
Web: http://yihui.name

messages.subject: putting lines in multiline LaTex equations in the PDF version of an Rmarkdown file
messages.subject_clean: putting lines in multiline LaTex equations in the PDF version of an Rmarkdown file
messages.body_plain:
Good morning!

First of all, knitr, Rmarkdown, and Rstudio are the best things since sliced bread, Coca-Cola, etc.

I have one questions, which I'm sure is an easy fix.

I am making up some lecture notes for my students.  Some like HTML, while others prefer PDF.  I like happy students.  So I am using Rmarkdown within Rstudio.

This is on a Mac, R Version 3.2.0.

Here are the lines from the Rmarkdown file:

We will review some of the very fun and interesting concepts that we discussed on Wednesday, August 26.

We know in our hearts that the gamma probability function is the following:

\[
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^r}{\Gamma(r)} x^{r-1} e^{-\lambda x},
\]

Here is some more stuff

\[
E[X] = \lambda \cdot \dfrac{\Gamma(2)}{\lambda^2}
 \left \lbrack \int_0^{\infty} \dfrac{\lambda^2}{\Gamma(2)}
x e^{-\lambda x} \; dx \right \rbrack, \\
E[X] = \lambda \cdot \dfrac{\Gamma(2)}{\lambda^2} \cdot 1, \\
E[X] = \dfrac{(2-1)!}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}
\]

This works just fine when I use knitr to HTML.  However, when I use knitr to PDF, the second set puts all of the equations on one line.

What can I do to fix this, please?

I also attached the entire file for ease of use.

Thank you for any help.

Sincerely,
Erin
